I'm delighted to be joined this afternoon with Luke Bourgeois from the Voyager Tennis Academy and before we get going into today's session, if I could just take a moment to acknowledge the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet, and if I could pay our respects to Elders past, present and future, and to any Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islanders who join us on the call this afternoon. So as I said, I'm joined today by Luke Bourgeois, who is the director of performance at the Voyager Tennis Academy, who were founded in 2011. They've been based in Sydney. Luke achieved an ATP singles ranking of 262, doubles ranking of 169, and was talented enough to be able to compete at all four slams in the juniors in doubles and in singles as well. And he comes fresh off another Newcombe awards win last night, so coaching of excellence in development of players, first one in 2017 and again in last night in the 2022 Newcombe medal. So congratulations, Luke. Maybe if we just, before we get going, maybe just talk a little bit about what the awards and what that means to you as an individual. Well, first of all, thanks, Lawrence. It's a pleasure to be here with you this afternoon. And yeah, it was a great night last night. Obviously super thrilled to be nominated, I guess, in the first place and acknowledged as a Newcombe medal winner. First of all, for TA, it's a great night, I mean, to bring together our entire sort of tennis community to be there to celebrate was fantastic. And so many people in that room were paid such a big part.

So, look, thanks for joining us today. We wanted to talk a little bit about UTR, which we know has been a big topic over the last 12 months and how Voyager have embraced that in terms of their player development program. And then more broadly into their into their business and hopefully provide some insights to coaches across the country as to how they look at building their own player development or squad programs and their business and how they can embrace it. But maybe before we get into the sort of nuts and bolts of it, can you just give a bit of an insight as to how you, Voyager, discovered UTR and when you first started to really embrace it in your business and in your programming and what was the, what was it that drove you to make that decision? Yeah, I mean, there's been so much talk about UTR recently, but it's been around for such a long time. I think it was founded in about 20 2008 or nine running in the background for a long, long time. And it's really around that U.S. college pathway. And we were first introduced through our partners at Study and Play USA. It was really around creating more competitive options. So we've actually been running UTR events probably now, I think probably close to eight or nine years. So we've been doing it for a very, very long time. And it's been from day one, it's always, I've always spoken to it. It's created match play with meaning. And that's one great thing that we've seen around about it, which is it's a way to really, again, know your level.

When you look at your player development, can you give me a little bit of an insight as to what you, Voyager, your ethos is towards match counts? What's the sort of guiding principle in terms of maybe a 12 or 14, 16 in terms of match counts and how do you try and identify and facilitate that meaningful match play for them? Yeah, I mean, so when we talk to this, it's really simple. I mean, we're not creating tennis trainers. We want to create tennis players and something I talk to is being prepared to play anyone at any time for anything and just getting out there and playing. And what we know is the players that are actually achieving the higher end levels that are kicking goals on an international level, their match count is generally very, very high. And this is one thing here where you look at it. It's created the platform for us to have those opportunities to play matches to get that match count. So what we look towards is to me about 100 for our full-time Academy players playing 120 competitive matches per year. So we aim for sort of 30 per quarter. And it was actually quite interesting. I was quite fortunate beyond the recent tour to the States with the Coach Acceleration Program going to the south of Florida and seeing where the IMGs, I mean, those kids are playing over 150 matches a year. And it's very, very clear to see, again, to come back, if you want to be a high end player and an elite player that's tournament tough, tournament ready, is you can't escape it.

So what one of the one of the questions I get asked regularly when I'm traveling, particularly to remote or regional areas is we don't have the depth of player that we might have in Sydney or a Melbourne or Brisbane. Where is my kids, my 14 or 15 year old kid who might be the the tall poppy in their environment like they're a really good kid. So if they look at the junior environment, there may not be the level of competition for them to be able to get the right level of hitting. As a coach in your player development mindset, when do you feel the right time is to have the conversation to say, we think you're ready to be playing. And I don't want to use of adult and junior, but we think you're ready to step into senior competition. We know that the rating gives an indication, but we've also heard from some parents and players. I don't want my 13 year old playing against a 25 year old that doesn't feel right. But if the rating is telling us that they're at a similar level as a coach and as a player developer, how do you have that conversation with the player and parent to say we think you're now ready to play in this environment because I think for our regional players, they're going to have to to get that match count. They're going to have to embrace midweek competition or whatever in order to get some of that match count up. Isn't this the beauty of tennis to me, the beauty of tennis is it's not age or gender specific. It really is about your level.
